extracted.intended_audience: community college faculty, administrators, and staff preparing grant proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for community college personnel on preparing competitive grant proposals that meet funder criteria, document need and partnerships, present specific plans and balanced budgets, and avoid common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet the Criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure that the proposal meets the criteria of the funding agency; careful reading of the restrictions and guidelines is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the directions exactly; failure to satisfy eligibility or stated objectives (for example, proposing projects for on-campus students under a program intended for off-campus community programs) is a fatal flaw. Proposals that do not meet the funder's rules are unlikely to be funded even if otherwise meritorious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present Specific Facts and Plans
rubrics_metrics.description: List specific classes, forums and seminars identified as to topic, cost, and duration rather than vague promises to offer programs 'to be determined.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators favor proposals that document specifics and verify need with external evidence (e.g., designations by private or governmental agencies, newspaper clippings, reprints). A program identified as addressing a community area designated by an outside agency as high-need is more persuasive than an unverified claim of need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Proposal Development a Year-Round Effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate continuously with community and college personnel about needs and maintain a 'proposal bank' reflecting ongoing identified needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals developed from sustained community contact (minutes of meetings, prior discussions) are stronger than last-minute ideas. Examples: successful projects have emerged from proposal files and earlier suggestions; including minutes from meetings held months before submission strengthens the case that the proposal responds to genuine, identified needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose Economic Solutions to Problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Design cost-effective interventions; avoid activities with high unit cost per participant when lower-cost local options exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare proposed costs to alternatives such as enrollment in regular local classes. Be cautious about proposing expensive consultants or flying in out-of-area experts—evaluators react negatively to unjustified high fees. The California Joint Legislative Audit Committee criticized excessive consultant use; justify necessity and reasonableness of consultant costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document the Involvement of Persons and Institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include supporting material (letters, resolutions) confirming participation of partner institutions and, when appropriate, short resumes of key personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the project involves a consortium, include letters from college presidents and resolutions of support from boards of trustees in the appendix. While projects (not people) are meant to be funded, the presence of highly qualified personnel or those with prior successes can positively influence reviewers—so include concise resumes when project success depends on specific individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple Check Your Figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify all numerical information—ensure budgets balance and calculations are correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors such as an unrealistic part-time position projecting an impossible full-time salary or unbalanced budgets damage credibility. Have financial officers (bursar/business manager) review budget figures for accuracy and internal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check Out the Proposal on Campus Before Submitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Have multiple disinterested, candid reviewers examine the proposal for language, accuracy, feasibility, and fundability before submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask English/journalism instructors to proofread grammar and usage; have the bursar review the budget; solicit candid reactions from readers who would tell you whether they would fund it if acting as external evaluators. Avoid only asking subordinates or those who may be reluctant to criticize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine Innovation and Appropriateness of Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming a program is 'new' or 'innovative,' ensure the claim is genuine and relevant rather than repackaging older ideas as innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overstating novelty; reviewers notice when 'innovations' are actually previously used approaches. Also avoid proposing 'in-house' solutions to problems that are external in nature—ensure the proposed response matches the community problem described.
